name: Kunal Lanjewar
bio: Kunal Lanjewar runs tier-zero infrastructure at Riot Games, where he builds and operates production AI agents and backend services that power games like VALORANT and League of Legends. He's the author of Guild, an open-source tool that gives AI agents persistent memory and task coordination across sessions. Previously, he helped scale Sky: Children of the Light to 300M+ downloads and millions of daily active players, and built the backend for its Guinness World Record-holding Aurora concert. His work has been featured at GDC, DataCon LA, and on the MongoDB Podcast. Earlier in his career he also built systems for NASA missions.

positions.claim: Traces are insufficient for understanding agent behavior because they are disconnected from the runtime and discard in-flight variables, filesystem state, and the executing code.
The industry lacks a clear connection between OpenTelemetry observability spans and the actual execution that produced them.
A new layer of the stack is emerging that sits above agent frameworks/harnesses and provides a durable runtime beneath them.
If a system already checkpoints in production, no additional data collection is needed to answer what-if questions about cost, latency, and quality.
Replay-based evaluation should use real production runs and checkpoints rather than synthetic datasets.
Simulations grounded in previously recorded executions are more trustworthy than ungrounded ones.
DoorDash reduced a multi-hour replay process to 5 minutes with hundreds of simulations, 90% fewer hallucinations, and results within two points of production.
Naive model swaps to cheaper models often fail in practice when evaluated on outcome quality rather than cost alone.
Optimizing on cost as a single dimension produces a false economy, per a BrainTrust study.
On τ-bench, a model that passes 60% of the time is self-consistent only about a quarter of the time.
A single replay is not evidence; decisions require cohort-level analysis.
Nothing should be shipped on the basis of one or two replays.
Analyzing replay cohorts at thousands-scale requires LLMs and agents, not human inspection of UI diffs.
Replay infrastructure must expose a queryable runtime that can fetch artifacts, so that MCP servers and skills can operate on it.
Replay at scale is expensive enough that selecting what to replay is itself a design problem.
The replay-and-decide loop should be automated, but a human should remain in the loop at the final decision point.
Whether a cheaper model is acceptable is data-dependent and cannot be generalized across deployments.
Coupling replay to the code base enables a wider range of experiments (such as mocking tools with real functions) than trace-only tooling allows.
